item.question_text: A team is mapping where risk can originate for an AI system it provides. Which statement best reflects the guidance in Annex C on life-cycle risk?

options.text: Risk can arise at any point, from design flaws through to problems at decommissioning.
Risk can arise mainly once the system meets production data, so monitoring is where it is found.
Risk can arise during design and build, and is closed out at the release gate.
Risk can arise chiefly in maintenance, where neglect accumulates after handover to operations teams.

item.explanation: C.3.6 treats the origins of risk as spread across the whole life cycle, illustrating this with examples that run from poor design, through deployment and neglected maintenance, to trouble at decommissioning. The other options narrow that span to a single stage.
item.key_support: Sources of risk can appear over the entire AI system life cycle (e.g. flaws in design, inadequate deployment, lack of maintenance, issues with decommissioning).

distractor_support.support: Sources of risk can appear over the entire AI system life cycle
distractor_support.why_wrong: It confines origination to the operational phase, whereas the clause names design flaws and decommissioning as well.

distractor_support.support: issues with decommissioning
distractor_support.why_wrong: Risk sources are described as continuing beyond release, including at decommissioning.

distractor_support.support: flaws in design, inadequate deployment, lack of maintenance
distractor_support.why_wrong: Lack of maintenance is only one example among several spread across the life cycle.

item.question_text: A deployed system goes on training its model using production data and output data while it is in service. What does the operation and monitoring guidance advise the organization to do?

options.text: Keep its performance under review so it goes on meeting the goals set at design.
Treat any change in behaviour as drift and retrain the model on a fixed schedule.
Rely on the acceptance testing done before release and then log errors and failures.
Ask users to report deviations through the support channel as the main check.

item.explanation: B.6.2.6 addresses continuously learning systems directly: "Where continuous learning is used, the organization should monitor the performance of the AI system to ensure that it continues to meet its design goals and operates on production data as intended." The guidance is advisory, and monitoring rests with the organization.
item.key_support: Where continuous learning is used, the organization should monitor the performance of the AI system to ensure that it continues to meet its design goals and operates on production data as intended.

distractor_support.support: The performance of some AI systems can change even if such systems do not use continuous learning, usually due to concept or data drift in production data.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Drift-driven retraining is the guidance for systems that do not learn continuously, not for this case.

distractor_support.support: Some deployed AI systems evolve their performance as a result of ML, where production data and output data are used to further train the ML model.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Because behaviour evolves in service, pre-release testing plus error logging is not what the guidance describes.

distractor_support.support: Support processes should consider how users can contact the appropriate help, how issues and incidents are reported, support service level agreements and metrics.
distractor_support.why_wrong: User support is a separate operational element and is not offered as the means of tracking learned behaviour.

item.question_text: A model that is never retrained in service shows falling accuracy because the production data has shifted. According to the operation and monitoring guidance, what can monitoring do in this situation?

options.text: It can surface a need to retrain so the system again meets its design goals.
It can show that continuous learning has altered the model's behaviour in service.
It can establish that the shift is a security event such as data poisoning.
It can confirm the system needs withdrawing until a fresh impact assessment is run.

item.explanation: B.6.2.6 states that where performance changes through concept or data drift, "monitoring can identify the need for retraining to ensure that the AI system continues to meet its design goals and operates on production data as intended".
item.key_support: In such cases, monitoring can identify the need for retraining to ensure that the AI system continues to meet its design goals and operates on production data as intended.

distractor_support.support: The performance of some AI systems can change even if such systems do not use continuous learning, usually due to concept or data drift in production data.
distractor_support.why_wrong: The scenario explicitly excludes continuous learning, so that mechanism does not explain the change.

distractor_support.support: AI-specific information security threats include, but are not limited to data poisoning, model stealing and model inversion attacks.
distractor_support.why_wrong: Data poisoning is treated as an information security threat, not as the explanation for concept or data drift.

distractor_support.support: monitoring can identify the need for retraining
distractor_support.why_wrong: The named response to drift is retraining, not withdrawal pending a new impact assessment.
